messages.subject_clean: Null/baseline model
messages.body_plain:
> I would like to know exactly how is defined the null / baseline model in lavaan. I tried to estimate a sem with no regressions at all, only the measurement model.

I think you are confusing different uses of the ambiguous term "baseline model".  It sounds like you are taking about a best-fitting model against which to compare more restricted models, as in comparing a restricted structural model among common factors (i.e., your latent regression model), compared to a CFA with unrestricted covariances among common factors (i.e., your measurement model).

The "baseline" model reported in summary() or fitMeasures() output is instead the "null" model that is used to calculate incremental fit indices such as CFI and TLI.  This is a worst-fitting model, not a best-fitting model.  For continuous data, the default null model in lavaan (and all other SEM software I am aware of) is the "independence" model, which constraints all covariances to zero, and only freely estimates means and variances.  To see the default version of the independence model for categorical data, you can inspect the parameter table lavaan uses.

> fit <- lavaan(...)
> lav_partable_independence(fit)

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

> Will lavaan understand this data orientation?

Whatever your sampling unit of interest is (e.g., occasions, individuals), lavaan expects data in wide format (one row per sampling unit).  It does not (yet) have features for analyzing multilevel data.  The lavaan.survey package can adjust standard errors for clustering, but I'm not sure whether that is relevant for you.

> Or should I reduce the dimensionality of my dataset and perform a principal component analysis for each of the test domains?

I'm not sure what that would accomplish.  A structural equation model is meant to represent a theoretical causal model, so the entities in the model should be real interpretable variables.  But this is beyond the scope of a software question.  SEMNET is available for general SEM questions, and hopefully someone in that wide audience could provide guidance on appropriate ways to use SEM for neuroimaging data.

messages.subject_clean: factor mean invariance with non-invariant intercepts
messages.body_plain:
Two items per factor with intercepts (and loadings) constrained to equality across groups can be sufficient to give meaning to differences in factor means (if they are the right two). Nine items per factor is more than enough. The item not constrained will not participate in defining the factor mean difference, but you do not need to discard the item, or the factor. The analysis is exploratory because you found the discrepant item with an ex post analysis, which raises the possibility of capitalizing on chance. But with 9 of 10 itme intercepts constrained to equality, I would wager that partial scalar invariance is well established. So carry on with the analysis, leaving the one item's intercept not constrained.
--Ed Rigdon

messages.subject_clean: factor mean invariance with non-invariant intercepts
messages.body_plain:
> "The item not constrained will not participate in defining the factor mean difference" can you explain why?

Latent variables are not observed, so we can only infer their distributional properties (means, variances) indirectly via their hypothesized effects on indicators.  We typically fix latent means for identification, but we can release those identification constraints (except for one group/occasion) when we constrain loadings and intercepts across groups/occasions.  When you constrain 5 out of 6 intercepts to equality, the differences in observed means of those 5 indicators between groups are assumed to be due only to differences in the common-factor means between groups. Because the 6th intercept is not constrained across groups, the observed means of the 6th indicator can differ not only because of common-factor mean differences, but also differences in the measurement parameters (intercepts).

This is a general SEM question, not specific to lavaan, so SEMNET would be a more appropriate forum to post this question.

I do not have a solution, only a strategy.  Here is what I would do in our situation:

1. Remove the bootstrapping.  Get the model to run first, then rerun it with bootstrapping.

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I have a question about constraining paths with groups, in what
appears to be a slightly unusual way.

I have a fixed-weighted-sum-scored "latent variable", and several
observed variables I want to regress onto the LV. I also have three
groups, which can be organized as 2 groups in 2 different ways (1
group overlaps with both other groups, but via different attributes
for each other group). The model definition is quite simple:

LV =~ 1*a1 + 1*a2 + 1*a3 + 1*a4 + 1*a5

LV ~ b1 + b2 + b3 + c1 + c2 + c3 + c4 + c5 +c6

Some of these variables are "of interest" - the c vars - and some are not - the b vars. The
not-interesting variables I want to include as controls, and for these
I want to allow their regression estimates onto the LV to be freely
estimated in all models - e.g., b1 ought to have a different
regression coefficient for each group.

At the same time, I want to be able to be able to have the of-interest c
regression coefficients jointly estimated, but not always jointly
estimated across all groups.

The syntax for estimating all three groups separately is simple enough:
lavaan(model=model, data=data, model.type='sem', group=3samples, ... )
Specify the groups, but don't specify anything to be equal.

Jointly estimating all parameters of-interest across the entire
dataset is easy too:
lavaan(model=model, data=data, model.type='sem', group=3samples,
 group.equal = c("regressions"), group.partial = c(LV ~ b1, ...), ...
 )

But if I want to jointly estimate coefficients for the c vars in 2 of the groups, and
estimate different c coefficients for the other group, while allowing
the b vars to be freely estimated ... Well, I have no idea how
to do this and I haven't been able to find anything while scouring the
web, either. I *think* this should at very least be doable
by specifying everything within the definition of the models,
but again, I don't know the syntax. Does anyone know how I should
go about this?

Many thanks,
                Drew

The answer may depend on which package you are using to load the dataset, but for example the haven package that RStudio uses when you import a dataset using menus does not automatically code missing data.

data <- as.data.frame(matrix(sample(c(1:5,99),100, replace = TRUE),20,5))

messages.subject_clean: Simulating non-normal ordinal data
messages.body_plain:
> Is it possible to simulate non-normal ordinal data with specific values of skewness and kurtosis using thresholds?

No, not by specifying the skew/kurtosis directly, since those values are calculated assuming the data are continuous.  You could do either of the following, depending on what you mean by "non-normal ordinal data"
Simulate non-normal latent item responses with chosen skew/kurtosis values, then discretize them to create your ordinal "observed" item responses.
Simulate data for which the normality assumption is met for the latent item responses, but choose asymmetric thresholds that make the histograms look non-normal.
(2) would require a little trial-and-error to find the skew/kurtosis values you want, by figuring out what the "mean" of the distribution would be for the ordinal items, as implied by the proportion of the population in each category.  For example, if 20% are 1s, 30% are 2s, 40% are 3s, and 10% are 4s, then the mean would be .2*1 + .3*2 + .4*3 + .1*4 = 2.4.  Then you can use the formulas found here <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skewness#Pearson.27s_moment_coefficient_of_skewness> and here <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurtosis#Pearson_moments> to calculate the 3rd- and 4th-order moments implied by the same proportions (e.g., 20% are 1 - 2.4 = -1.4 away from the mean, 30% are 2 - 2.4 = -0.4 away from the mean, etc.).

If you want to use some thresholds from a previous simulation study, here is an example (see p. 170):

http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2014.882658

Hi,

You are regressing speed on textual and visual, and that R2 of speed is from that regression. Visual and textual are exogenous variables, so they do not have R2 values. R2 is a measure of variance explained by a set of variables. But that you probably know already. If you want to get the amount of variance explained uniquely by visual and textual, you need to look into different effect size statistics. The choice of effect size statistic depends on what exactly you want to quantify. See this article for an introduction

Kelley, K., & Preacher, K. J. (2012). On effect size. Psychological Methods, 17(2), 137.

As a side note, you should probably use the sem function instead of the cfa function when fitting models with latent regressions.

messages.subject: Suggestion of further development
messages.subject_clean: Suggestion of further development
messages.body_plain:
Dear Yves,

I greatly appreciate your work! lavaan is definitely a wonderful gift to the community of researchers around the world.

May I make a suggestion if this is not in the list of future development?

As we know, the usual purpose of SEM is to make sense of relationships among manifest variables (MVs) based on a theory about latent variables (LVs). In most situations, scales of variables (not only LVs but even MVs) are not of primary interest, and this is why some people who know what SEM is about want to just look at standardized parameters and their corresponding SEs and CIs. For example, RAMONA in SYSTAT, an SEM software package that people no longer use much but is otherwise technically meticulous, reports all standardized parameters *along with* their correct SEs, CIs, and test statistics.

With lavaan, this is not possible. Note that correct SEs and CIs for parameters with all variables standardized are not obtained simply by applying some formulas to fitted results. The parameterization should be different in order to obtain correct results. The idea (which is implemented in RAMONA, for example) is that equality constrains are imposed on the variances of all endogenous variables (both LVs and MVs). Of course, you cannot directly set them to 1 since they are endogenous. Instead, these constraints are imposed on the parameters influencing the endogenous variables. In the case of MVs, you need to insert sort of pseudo-LVs as indicators of each MV and estimate nuisance factor loadings to account for MVs' variances. The residual variances of MVs are set to 0, and instead, error terms are attached to these pseudo-LVs.

As far as I know, this is the only way to obtain correct SEs and CIs for fully standardized parameters.

-Jae

P.S. Not only that, the current way of standardizing endogenous LVs in lavaan make parameters around them difficult to interpret.

> In fact, in typical applications of SEM, we are concerned about standardized coefficients as scales do not matter. That is why SEM software should provide an option that outputs CIs for standardized parameters.

There is an option:

?bootstrapLavaan()

You can use the bootstrap CI as a measure of uncertainty about the estimate, or you can just use the SE from the standardizedSolution() output to measure uncertainty.  But if you want to use the CI as an inverted hypothesis test (to answer the question: With which parameters are my data consistent? or Which null hypotheses could I not reject), the typical null hypothesis of 0 applies just as easily to an unstandardized vs. standardized estimate. messages.subject_clean: Second-Order Multi-Group Latent Growth Model: Model fitting issues
messages.body_plain:
> how can the parcel-intercepts be higher than the maximum of the scale (7)?

An endogenous variable's intercept is its estimated marginal mean when each of its predictors == 0.  If your indicator intercepts are outside the range of observed values, then 0 is probably outside the range of values for its predictor(s).  In this case, the only predictor of each indicator is its common factor, and the common factors all have means of 0.998 (at T1) or greater (because the slope is positive, as are the slope loadings for T2 and T3).  Given how small the variances are for the common factors, a value of 0 would be many SDs below the mean, so the intercepts for the indicators are the conditional means of those variables for very atypical values on the common factors.

> Shouldn't the Second Order Intercept be in range of the population mean (which is around 3.5), but not near zero?

Not necessarily.  First, you used the identification constraint of fixing the common-factor intercepts to zero.  If you used a marker variable to identify the mean structure (i.e., fixing the first indicator's intercept == 0), like you did for the covariance structure (i.e., fixing the first indicator's loading == 1), then your model-implied latent means should be in the familiar 1-7 range (not that those variables would be on a 1-7 scale).  But the estimated growth-factor intercepts might still be outside that range, depending on the observed values of the covariate that predicts the growth factors.  Again, an endogenous variable's intercept is its estimated marginal mean when each of its predictors == 0.  So if zero is outside the range of observed values for the covariate, then the growth-factor intercepts are conditional on values that do not apply to your sample.  To solve that "problem", you could center the covariate at a meaningful value, or the minimum observed value, or the mean.

> Several negative variances in several groups show that something is wrong with my model. But what? Is the number of observations to small?

Possibly related to the hidden proportionality assumption in the latent-basis curve.  It is not as "unrestricted" as people think:

http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2014.938578

> Or is this more a question for SEMNET?

SEMNET would be a good place to post questions like this, because they are not software-specific.

> Is it possible to manually set parameters equal for specific groups (e.g. group 1 and 2) but not for others using the "group.equal" comand?

No, that is just a shortcut.  Better to specify constraints manually with labels in the syntax

http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/syntax2.html

messages.body_plain:
> packages or ready-made routines to do multiple imputation for exploratory factor analysis? Particularly when one has ordered categorical data. I was checking on semTools but it seems it only has a function for CFA.

Indeed, the runMI() function and efaUnrotate() functions in semTools were not designed to cooperate.  But efaUnrotate() is just a shortcut for specifying EFA models as CFA models (i.e., all indicators load on all common factors, no residual covariances, orthogonal common factors), which is something you can do manually.  If you specify the "EFA" models manually (one each for the number of factors you want to test extracting), then you can fit each to your list of imputed data sets using runMI().

Or you can get the model specifications "automatically" from efaUnrotate() by using it on the first imputed data set, once for each number-of-factors you want to extract.  Once you have those fitted models (which are lavaan models), you can extract the parameter table from each one to use as the "model" argument in runMI() instead of model syntax. Here's an example for a 3-factor solution (assuming you use Amelia, which is arbitrary).

> impOut <- amelia(myData, m = 20, ords = ...)
> impList <- impOut$ imputations
> ## get model specification for a 3-factor solution
> PT3 <- parTable(efaUnrotate(impList[[1]], nf = 3, ordered = ...)
> ## fit model to imputed data sets
> out3 <- cfa.mi(PT3, data = impList, ordered = ...)

> Is there a way to set up a generic lavaan model that will import a value from outside lavaan?

Not like that.  Previous posts on this forum have talked about 2 methods:
using the paste() function to specify the skeleton of your model syntax, with variables for the values you want to paste into the syntax
creating a parameter table from the syntax, then updating the value(s) in the parameter table (which is a data.frame; see ?parTable and ?lavaanify).

> model <- ' y1 ~ a*x1 + b*x2 '
> fit <- lavaan(model, data, constraints = c('a == .5','b == .6'), ...)

Of course, you can still use paste() to make the constraints.

> myParams <-

> fit <- lavaan(model, data, constraints = myConstraints, ...)

Am Montag, 20. Februar 2017 11:44:31 UTC+1 schrieb Terrence Jorgensen:
> > how can the parcel-intercepts be higher than the maximum of the scale (7)?
>
> An endogenous variable's intercept is its estimated marginal mean when each of its predictors == 0.  If your indicator intercepts are outside the range of observed values, then 0 is probably outside the range of values for its predictor(s).  In this case, the only predictor of each indicator is its common factor, and the common factors all have means of 0.998 (at T1) or greater (because the slope is positive, as are the slope loadings for T2 and T3).  Given how small the variances are for the common factors, a value of 0 would be many SDs below the mean, so the intercepts for the indicators are the conditional means of those variables for very atypical values on the common factors.
>
> > Shouldn't the Second Order Intercept be in range of the population mean (which is around 3.5), but not near zero?
>
> Not necessarily.  First, you used the identification constraint of fixing the common-factor intercepts to zero.  If you used a marker variable to identify the mean structure (i.e., fixing the first indicator's intercept == 0), like you did for the covariance structure (i.e., fixing the first indicator's loading == 1), then your model-implied latent means should be in the familiar 1-7 range (not that those variables would be on a 1-7 scale).  But the estimated growth-factor intercepts might still be outside that range, depending on the observed values of the covariate that predicts the growth factors.  Again, an endogenous variable's intercept is its estimated marginal mean when each of its predictors == 0.  So if zero is outside the range of observed values for the covariate, then the growth-factor intercepts are conditional on values that do not apply to your sample.  To solve that "problem", you could center the covariate at a meaningful value, or the minimum observed value, or the mean.
>
> > Several negative variances in several groups show that something is wrong with my model. But what? Is the number of observations to small?
>
> Possibly related to the hidden proportionality assumption in the latent-basis curve.  It is not as "unrestricted" as people think:
>
> http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2014.938578 <http://www.google.com/url?q=http%3A%2F%2Fdx.doi.org%2F10.1080%2F10705511.2014.938578&sa=D&sntz=1&usg=AFQjCNHVQ2ribBteADILnh9CXvfm2WRfBg>
>
> > Or is this more a question for SEMNET?
>
> SEMNET would be a good place to post questions like this, because they are not software-specific.
>
> > Is it possible to manually set parameters equal for specific groups (e.g. group 1 and 2) but not for others using the "group.equal" comand?
>
> No, that is just a shortcut.  Better to specify constraints manually with labels in the syntax
>

messages.body_plain:
> if we see some sort of asymmetry in the observed proportions it could either come because the latent distribution is skewed and the thresholds are evenly-spaced OR the distribution is indeed normal but the thresholds are uneven.

Correct, and it can get even more complicated.  It is possible that both are true (asymmetric thresholds AND nonnormal latent item-response).  If the latent-response distribution is nonnormal, is that because that latent common factor is nonnormal, or because the residuals are nonnormal?  Again, it could be both, especially if important 3rd variables are omitted from the model (e.g., bimodal common-factor and/or latent-response distributions due to sex differences).

> But, in reality, there is no way of knowing... is there?

No, these are among the assumptions we have to make in order to draw inferences.  Regardless of the method we use, our inferences will always be conditional on "if our assumptions are met, then..."

> Would it make any difference to simulate data one way or the other?

Although I have seen studies implement one or the other of these methods, I haven't seen a study directly comparing both methods. I would be interested in reading such a study, because the two methods of simulating data represent two very different real-world scenarios.
Simulating normal item responses and discretizing them with asymmetric thresholds is technically not a violation of any assumption.  Thresholds are chosen from a (standard) normal distribution, so if latent item responses are normal, the assumption is met.  But in practice, more asymmetric thresholds have been shown to yield inflated Type I error rates (again, even though assumptions were met):  http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2014.859510
Simulating nonnormal item responses means that the thresholds chosen from a normal distribution do not apply, even if those are the ones used to discretize the data.  The estimated thresholds will be the ones that return model-implied proportions in each response category assuming the latent response is normal, not the thresholds you actually used to simulated data.  I think this method of simulating "skewed"-looking ordinal data only makes sense if you are concerned with situations when you would not expect a normally distributed continuous response, even if you used a more sensitive measurement instrument (e.g., a 0-10 scale) that could be treated as continuous.

messages.body_plain:
Conal,

In this context 'variance' does not just mean variability, it means the square of the standard deviation.

Reliability is an estimate of r[x,x'].  If you think of it like a path diagram, r[x, x'] decomposes into r[x,T] * r[x', T].  However, one can assume that these are equal.  So, the expression simplifies to r[x,T]^2.  One can also interpret as a coefficient of determination giving the proportion of the variance in x explained by the true score T.

Based on the above, we can decompose the variance of x, S[x], into two parts:  r[x, x'] * S[x] is the portion of the variance in x explained by T.  The remainder of the variance in x, (1 - r[x, x']) * S[x], represents the unexplained part.  You are fixing the unique variance in the structural equation model to equal this estimated unexplained variance.

This only works for one indicator.  With more than one, the random error of classical test theory offers only a lower bound to the unique variance for an indicator.  With only one indicator, the latent variable variance is not common to a set of items.  So, it is safer to think of the unique variance as random error in the single indicator case.

None of this says anything about validity, of course.  Your estimate of r[x, x'] is for whatever the item measures, not necessarily what you meant it to measure.  Your intended interpretation does not fit into the formula for alpha in any way.

My recommendation would be to run the model with a few different values.  For example, calculate the 95% CI around alpha and try the two bounds of the CI as well.  Think of this as a sensitivity analysis.  If the differences do not greatly affect the rest of your model, then you can feel more confident in the results.  Perhaps just mention the sensitivity analysis in a footnote.  If the results do vary appreciably, then it may be a good idea to more fully incorporate the sensitivity analysis into your reporting of the results.

None of this is specific to lavaan.

Keith

DWLS is an asymptotic estimation method, performing worse than MLE does at moderate sample size with continuous data. messages.subject_clean: Multi-Level CFA
messages.body_plain:
> I am currently attempting to learn multi-level reliability for scales.

That is a complex topic.  Consider adding this to your reading list:

Geldhof, J. G., Preacher, K. J., & Zyphur, M. J. (2014). Reliability estimation in a multilevel confirmatory factor analysis framework. Psychological Methods, 19(1), 72–91. doi:10.1037/a0032138

> I want to try and replicate the study [1] where the author suggests to implement the following steps. The aim is to see at what level of measurement an analysis is most effective. In this paper the auther aims to prove that people should analysis the Data in GLOBE not on individual level but on societal level. He then goes about proving this showing the loadings on societal level are far higher than on individual level

By definition, that must be the case if loadings are approximately equal across clusters (metric invariance across clusters implies equal loadings at the between and within levels).  And if strong measurement invariance holds exactly, that implies zero residual variance at the between level (so standardized factor loadings will be close to 1 when strong invariance holds approximately).

Jak, S., Oort, F. J., & Dolan, C. V. (2013). A test for cluster bias: Detecting violations of measurement invariance across clusters in multilevel data. Structural Equation Modeling, 20(2), 265–282. doi:10.1080/10705511.2013.769392

So higher standardized loadings at the between level don't necessarily imply that the construct has more meaning or is "measured better" at that level.  The reliability you should be interested in is the reliability at the level of measurement about which you have other research questions.

>
> "Step 1: perform a conventional confirmatory factor analysis on the sample total covariance"
> "Step 2: estimate between-group level variation"
> "Step 3: perform a factor analysis on the sample pooled-within covariance matrix"
> "Step 4: perform a factor analysis on the sample between-group covariance matrix"
> "Step 5: perform multilevel confirmatory factor analysis"
>
>
> Im relatively new to SEM and CFA and like using the lavaan package very much. It appears the authors of this paper used MPlus
>
> Is it possible to have this workflow in lavaan using R? I see in page two of the manual [2] that lavaan provides "support for hierarchical/multilevel datasets (multilevel cfa, multilevel sem)". I have not been able to fin any tutorial on it

The material you quoted is a bullet point under the text of what is "currently NOT available in lavaan".  But multilevel support is on its way.  It will not be implemented the Mplus way, though, but the GLLAMM <http://www.gllamm.org/> way.   Regardless of whether you can use the same workflow, that 12-year-old advice is not necessarily the best to follow.  MSEM is a rapidly developing field, and we are still learning about the full implications of things like constraints across clusters and across levels of measurement.  Here are some more recent readings:

Stapleton, L. M., Yang, J. S., & Hancock, G. R. (2016). Construct meaning in multilevel settings. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, 41(5), 481–520. doi:10.3102/1076998616646200

Tay, L., Woo, S. E., & Vermunt, J. K. (2014). A conceptual and methodological framework for psychometric isomorphism validation of multilevel construct measures. Organizational Research Methods, 17(1), 77–106. doi:10.1177/1094428113517008

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
> I saw the mimic ="eqs" option on the fit function and I was wondering if there was a way to specify the elliptical model using the existing family of estimators supported by lavaan.

mimic ="eqs" only tells lavaan to make some output similar to EQS (e.g., how to calculate standardized residuals and SRMR, whether to use N or (N - 1) when calculating SEs and chi-squared).  According to p. 8 of the EQS manual, elliptical estimation is unique to EQS, but it is just another form of weighted least squares (WLS) with a particular weight matrix.  If you can figure out how to calculate that weight matrix (WLS.V) with the rows/columns arranged as lavaan expects (see ?lavaan help page), you can pass it to lavaan:

myWeightMatrix <- { something amazing }
fit <- lavaan(model = mySyntax, data = myData,
              estimator = "WLS", WLS.V = myWeightMatrix)

Terrence D. Jorgensen

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

Alex
